headline: UK plans social media curfew for 16-17 year olds, blocking apps midnight-6am by default
summary: The UK's new rules will impose a default social media block for 16-17 year olds from midnight to 6 am, though it can be overridden. This is alongside a total ban for under-16s by 2027 and a crackdown on 'addictive' features.
details: The United Kingdom will require social media companies to implement a default block for adolescent users aged 16 and 17 at certain hours. This automatic curfew would theoretically lock older teens out of social platforms between midnight and 6 am, though the feature can be turned off.

This nonmandatory restriction is to be imposed along with a looming total ban on these services for children under 16, expected to come into force in spring 2027. Both measures follow the Online Safety Act, which requires platforms hosting potentially harmful material to verify users are 18 or older.

Young Brits will also see a 'crackdown' on 'addictive' features of social apps, including videos that automatically play one after another and feeds that continually serve up personalized content. These mechanisms will be switched off by default for older teenagers, but users will also be able to override them.

The first full set of social media regulations will be put to Parliament later this year before taking effect in 2027. The Department for Science, Innovation & Technology (DSIT) stated these regulations aim to ensure a smooth transition in protections as young people move into their later teenage years.

UK Technology Secretary Liz Kendall said these measures will be crucial in helping young people get the sleep they need, focus on school, and spend more quality time with family and friends. She added that the goal is for young people to enjoy technology's benefits while having tools to thrive online.

The DSIT further signaled that Kendall aims to bring forth additional protections around artificial intelligence, including mandated chatbot breaks for children under 18. Regulators will be charged with reining in services that provide dangerous, misleading, or unverified mental health advice.

Chatbots found to 'pose a serious threat' to UK youths may be banned altogether. Additionally, the government is seeking to bolster children’s media literacy with updated school curricula covering AI, technological bias, and strategies for identifying violent and misogynist content.

These moves come as tech giants face lawsuits and research related to social media's negative effects on younger users. About 9 in 10 UK parents support a legal requirement for social media services to have a minimum age of access.

However, groups including the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the American Civil Liberties Union have criticized 'age-gating.' They argue it's an oversimplified solution that curtails rights to open information and free speech, potentially censoring vital resources for teens.

Enforcement also poses a challenge, as seen in Australia, which banned children under 16 from popular social media apps in December. Early research shows around 75% of 14- to 15-year-olds are circumventing the age limit there.

headline_marked: [[Meta sued over AI-fueled layoffs]] allegedly targeting disabled workers and those on leave
headline: Meta sued over AI-fueled layoffs allegedly targeting disabled workers and those on leave
summary: A new lawsuit alleges Meta used internal AI systems, including 'Metamate', to select 8,000 employees for termination, disproportionately affecting those with disabilities or on protected medical/family leave.
details: A lawsuit filed by 26 former employees alleges Meta used internal AI tools to select 8,000 workers for termination. The complaint claims these systems disproportionately targeted employees with disabilities and those who took protected medical or family leaves. Meta denies these claims, stating decisions were made by people.

The lawsuit specifies several internal AI systems, including 'Metamate,' "employee-trained 'second-brain' agents," keystroke and activity-monitoring data, and AI-token-usage dashboards. These tools were used for algorithmic performance ranking and calibration.

Employees were allegedly classified by their adoption stage of Meta's AI tools, with categories like 'AI Native' and 'AI First'. The lawsuit claims performance inputs from these tools could not be accumulated by employees on leave or with reduced output due to disability.

This legal challenge is reportedly the first against a major US company to contest the alleged use of AI in conducting layoffs. The plaintiffs argue Meta's monitoring tools did not account for differences caused by disabilities or protected leaves.

The complaint states Meta did not adjust scores for employees on protected leave or seeking accommodations, nor did it exclude them from the selection cohort. This allegedly penalized employees for exercising their legal rights to these leaves.

Meta issued a statement to Ars Technica, asserting, "These claims lack merit and are not based on facts. Workforce management and organizational decisions were and are made by people, not AI." The company offered no further comment.

The lawsuit highlights cases such as a scientist selected for layoff while on approved pre-birth pregnancy leave, just days before giving birth. Other plaintiffs were on maternity, paternity, or medical leave for disabilities. Some had returned to work under approved work-from-home accommodations that remained in effect when they were selected for termination.
The 26 plaintiffs had requested leaves or disability accommodations within 24 months prior to their selection for layoffs. The terminations, though not finalized, are scheduled to begin on July 22.

These cuts followed an internal memo from Chief People Officer Janelle Gale, announcing a 10% workforce reduction and a hiring freeze. This occurred despite Meta reporting record revenue and committing billions to AI investments.
